Stickle 2, Chong Fang 1, Cong Liu 2, Jun Lu 3,⇑, Xiulei Ji 1,⇑ 1 Department of Chemistry, Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, United States 2 Hewlett-Packard Co., 1000 NE Circle Blvd., Corvallis, OR, United States 3 Chemical Sciences and Engineering Division, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, IL, United States Practical lithium-sulfur batteries stipulate the use of a lean-electrolyte and a high Coulombic efficiency of the lithium metal anode.
Herein, we employ 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl ether as a co-solvent in the electrolyte of Li-S batteries to meet the demands.
The co-solvent fosters the formation of a LiF-rich solid electrolyte interphase on lithium metal anode, as revealed by Ab initio molecular dynamics and Femtosecond Stimulated Raman spectroscopy.
The co-solvent results in an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.4% for lithium plating/stripping cycles.

Full cells with a capacity ratio of 2 between lithium anode and the S@PAN cathode (3 mgs cm2) exhibited a stable cycle life over 100 cycles at an electrolyte/sulfur ratio of 2 mL mg1, validating the high Coulombic efficiency of the lithium anode and demonstrating the compatibility of the electrolyte with both electrodes.
To enhance the energy density, we prepared a hybrid cathode composed of 45 wt.% VS2 mixed with ZnS-coated Li2S@graphene as the cathode.
Based on the mass of both electrodes and the electrolyte, the full cell delivers an energy density of 483 Wh kg1, which demonstrates viable Li-S batteries with the leanelectrolyte.
Introduction Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries represent a promising nextgeneration high-energy battery technology [1].
Recently, a plethora of examples of high-performing Li-S cells have been demonstrated [2–4].

However, commercialization of Li-S batteries still confronts several major technical challenges, including the shuttling of polysulfide species [5], rapid capacity fading of the sulfur cathode under lean-electrolyte conditions [6], and the low Coulombic efficiency (CE) of plating/stripping of the lithium metal anode (LMA) [7], where the latter two issues can be the real showstoppers but have received meager effort, to date [8–13].

Remarkable advances have been made in polysulfide immobilization by, for example, intricate carbon/sulfur nano-composites [14,15], coated separators [16,17], and highly concentrated electrolytes [18,19].

These strategies are efficacious in electrolyteflooded Li-S systems; however, the superlative results often fail to be translated under the lean-electrolyte conditions, where the sulfur cathode accentuates much lower capacity and fast fading [20].
Note that the inconveniently necessary but extravagant usage of electrolyte tanks the specific energy of the Li-S cells and raises the manufacturing cost [21,22].
Besides the challenge to secure the high performance of cathode, the lean electrolyte needs to facilitate the impeccably reversible plating and stripping cycles of LMA.

Unfortunately, conventional electrolytes used by the LIB industry is unstable with LMA, both thermodynamically and kinetically, resulting in continuous corrosion of LMA and the formation of lithium dendrites [7].

to identify electrolytes that are kinetically stable with LMA via passivation with solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) under lean conditions [23,24].

Most recently, strides of progress have been made to enhance the performance of sulfur electrodes under lean-electrolyte conditions, i.e., at an electrolyte/sulfur (E/S) ratio of 5 (mL mg1) or below [25–28].
Hollow current collectors [29], swellable sulfur cathode [30], and ZnS-coating [31] were employed for the enhanced electrolyte uptake.
Modifications of electrolytes have also been made.

For instance, dimethyl disulfide is used as a co-solvent for a higher discharge capacity [32]; catholyte comprising Li2S6 facilitated electrolyte permeation into thick sulfur electrodes [33]; a salt of NH4TFSI served as a redox enhancer to alleviate Li2S passivation, thus promoting the S/Li2S utilization [20].
Electrocatalysts such as vacancy-rich Ni3FeN were utilized to improve surface reactions of sulfide species [34].
Electrolyte represents the centrality to improve the CE of LMA.
Recently, multiple localized high concentration electrolytes (LHCE) were introduced [35–39].
These low-viscosity electrolytes are usually fluorine rich, which facilitates the formation of SEI passivation layers on LMA.

For instance, Nazar and coworkers developed a LHCE that contained 1,1,2,2- tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (HFE) in diglyme (G2), which delivered a CE of 96.2% for LMA, and in this electrolyte the S/CMK-3 cathode exhibited 100 cycles at an E/S ratio of 5 at 55 C [35].

Liang and coworkers used a mixture electrolyte comprising hexa-fluoroisopropyl methyl ether (HFME), ethylene carbonate (EC), and diethyl carbonate (DEC), which achieved a CE of 99.5% for LMA and 50 cycles for the S/Ketjen black cathode at an E/S ratio of 1.5 [36].

In a similar fashion, Wang and coworkers employed a mixture of 1H,1H,5H-octafluoropentyl-1 ,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl ether (OFE) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) with the volume ratio of 95:5 and an E/S ratio of around 4.8, where the CE of LMA reached 99.3%, and the sulfur cathode retained a discharge capacity of 775 mAh g1 at the 150th cycle with the active mass loading of 1–2 mgs cm2 [37].
To date, lean electrolytes have been reported in half cells either for the sulfur electrode or for the LMA separately.
However, it is rarely reported that under lean-electrolyte conditions, an electrolyte can facilitate both high CE of LMA and stable cycling of the Li-S batteries at the full-cell level.

Herein, we report a new electrolyte formula for Li-S batteries under lean conditions, where 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,2- trifluoroethyl ether (TFTFE, Scheme 1) is employed as a cosolvent added to the electrolyte of 6 M lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) in DME.
TFTFE outperforms other recently reported fluorinated ethers in safety, and its cost and purity are competitive (Table S1).
TFTFE was used as an electrolyte for Li- S batteries by Liu and co-workers owing to the its unique inertness against polysulfides [40].
TFTFE was later reported as a cosolvent mixed with the electrolytes of fluorinated carbonates in a lithium metal battery with a NMC811 cathode [41].

In this study, we demonstrate that the TFTFE/DME/LiFSI electrolyte is highly compatible with LMA, where the average plating/stripping CE reaches 99.4% over 350 cycles, and the sulfur cathode delivers stable cycling performance under the lean-electrolyte conditions with E/S ratios of as low as 2.

Furthermore, femtosecond stimulated Raman spectroscopy (FSRS) and Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations reveal that the TFTFE addition does not alter the solvation structure of the electrolyte salt but profoundly affects the electrochemical performance of both electrodes.

When a S@PAN cathode and a limited mass of LMA with the anode/cathode capacity (N/P) ratio of 2 are assembled in full cells with the lean electrolyte at an E/S ratio of 2, the full cell with the S@PAN cathode delivered 100 cycles without a glitch.

In addition, pairing the electrolyte with a hybrid sulfur cathode that has 45 wt.% vanadium disulfide (VS2) added into a cathode of ZnS-coated Li2S@graphene, the same full cell configuration demonstrated one of the highest energy densities of 483 Wh kg1 based on the mass of both and electrolyte.
Lastly, this electrolyte exhibits low viscosity for excellent electrode wetting and anti-flammable properties for enhanced battery safety.
Materials and methods Electrolyte and cathode preparation The baseline electrolyte (BE) is 6 M LiFSI (99%, Oakwood Chemicals) in DME (99.5%, anhydrous, Sigma Aldrich).
The salt was dried at 95 C under Ar to remove trace water before use.
The mixture of salt and solvent was stirred for 3 h.
The diluent, TFTFE (99%, SynQuest Labs), was added to the as-prepared BE (BE/ TFTFE, v/v 1:2 or 1:5) to prepare hybrid electrolytes, HE-2 and HE-5, respectively.
S@PAN cathode was synthesized as previously reported [42].
Briefly, acrylonitrile (99%, Sigma Aldrich) and sublimed sulfur (99.98%, Sigma Aldrich) were mixed in a mass ratio of 1:4 and ball milled for an hour.
Homogeneously mixed powder was annealed at 450 C for 3 h under N2 at a ramping rate of 5 C min1.

A hybrid cathode powder was synthesized in three steps and all moisture/oxygen sensitive syntheses were conducted in a tube-furnace housed in a glovebox under Ar: (1) Li2S@graphene nanocapsules were synthesized as reported [43].
Briefly, lithium foil (0.38 mm in thickness, Alfa Aesar) was placed in the tube furnace, and CS2 liquid in a flask was bubbled by Ar to form a mixture gas containing CS2 vapor.
This gas passed through the quartz tube as ramping up the temperature to 650 C, and this temperature was held for five hours, followed by naturally cooling down to room temperature.
(2) The obtained Li2S@graphene was finely ground using mortar/pestle, then it was gently pressed to form a pellet.

The Zn precursor suspension, a mixture of 50 mg zinc acetylacetonate and 5 mL of dimethylformamide (DMF), was dropped on the pellet, which was dried under vacuum for 5 h to remove solvent before it was transferred to a tube furnace.

Annealing was conducted at 650 C for 3 h under the flow of Ar/ CS2 mixture gas to obtain ZnS-coated Li2S@graphene.
The powder was collected after the pellet was naturally cooled down.
(3) VS2 was prepared by the method as reported [44].
Briefly, 1.2 g Na3VO412H2O and thioacetamide were mixed in de-ionized water, followed by heating up to 160 C for 24 h in a Teflon autoclave.
Once it was naturally cooled down, it was centrifuged and rinsed with de-ionized water and ethanol several times before use.
Electrode preparation For the S@PAN electrode, slurry was made by mixing the active material, conductive carbon (C-45), and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVdF) binder at a mass ratio of 80:10:10.
A hybrid cathode slurry was prepared by mixing the VS2, ZnS-coated Li2S@graphene, C- 45, and PVdF at a mass ratio of 45:45:5:5 with N-Methyl-2- Pyrrolidone (NMP) as a solvent.
Slurry was casted on the carbon-coated Al foil (15 mm thickness, MTI) and dried at 65 C overnight.
The dried electrode film was punched into circular disks with an area of 0.76 cm2.
Cell fabrication The 2032-type coin cells were used for Li||Cu cell and Li||Li cells.
In a Li||Cu cell, Li metal foil was used as the counter and reference electrode, and Cu foil (MTI) was used as working electrode.

In both cells, regular polypropylene separators (25 mm, Celgard 2400) were employed for HE-2, whereas hydrophilic polypropylene separators (25 mm, Celgard 3501) were applied for BE to enhance wettability.
All cell fabrication was conducted inside Ar-filled glovebox, where O2 and H2O concentrations are below 10 ppm.

Materials characterization A home-built wavelength-tunable femtosecond stimulated Raman spectroscopy (FSRS) setup [45,46] was used to collect the experimental Raman spectra on the basis of a femtosecond (fs) Ti:sapphire laser amplifier system (Mantis-5 and Legend Elite-USP-1 K-HE, Coherent, Inc.).
Fundamental output of 800 nm center wavelength, 35 fs pulse duration, 4 mJ pulse energy, and 1 kHz repetition rate were applied.
SEM images of the deposited/cycled Li electrodes were obtained with Quanta 600 FEG SEM with an accelerating voltage of 5 kV.

Electrochemical tests A Maccor battery tester (Maccor) was used to perform all electrochemical coin-cell tests including plating/stripping of Li for the Li||Cu systems and galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD) for half-cell and full cell tests in coin cells.
For plating, a current density of 0.5 mA cm2 was applied for 2 h before stripping at a same current density until the potential reached 1.0 V.
In a Li||Li symmetric cell test, current densities of 0.5 mA cm2, 1.0 mA cm2, and 2.0 mA cm2 were applied for 20 cycles with a capacity of 1.0 mAh cm2.
Then it was switched back to 0.5 mA cm2 for another 20 cycles.
Theoretical calculations AIMD calculations were carried out using the Vienna ab initio simulation Package (VASP) [47,48].
Generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) [49] exchange–correlation functional was used, in conjunction with the projector augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotentials.
Initial geometries of solutions were generated by randomly mixing salt and solvent molecules using the Packmol software [50].
Number of atoms, volume of a virtual cell, and temperature at 363 K (NVT) were maintained during the calculation.
An energy cutoff of 500 eV with a Monhrost-Pack [51] reciprocal space grid of 1  1  1 k-points scheme was used.
The time step was 1 fs, and the snapshot at 13 ps was used to study Li-solvation structure analysis.
The radial distribution function (RDF) was generated using VMD [52].

Results and discussion We set 6 M LiFSI in DME as the baseline electrolyte (BE) and mixed it with TFTFE in two volume ratios, v/v 1:2 and 1:5, resulting in two hybrid electrolytes, referred to as HE-2 and HE-5.
When adding a co-solvent, the first question is whether it participates in the solvation structures of electrolyte ions.
To learn the interactions between the electrolyte species, we conducted FSRS measurements (Figure 1a).

Pure DME exhibits integrated vibration modes at 820 and 850 cm1 that are ascribed to the free ethylene oxide [53], and pure TFTFE shows vibrations at FIGURE 1 Coordination structures of electrolytes.
(a) Raman spectra display that the coordination environment of electrolyte constituents is not altered by TFTFE dilution.
(b) AIMD of BE and HE-2 electrolytes, showing that Li+ binds more strongly with FSI at a high concentration and retains its preference despite the presence of TFTFE.

648 cm1 and 850 cm1 attributed to -CF2 wagging and asymmetric C-O stretching, respectively [54,55].

For a controlled electrolyte of 2 M LiFSI solvated in DME, the peak at 717 cm1 indicates the S-N-S stretching vibration mode of FSI [56], which shifts to 735 cm1 when the concentration of LiFSI increases to 6 M in BE due to more prolific pairing between FSI and Li+ [57].
At the same time, the DME peak also shifts from 827 cm1 to 867 cm1 due to the enhanced interaction of DME with Li+ while the stretch of free DME molecules vanishes.
A peak separation was observed between 825 cm1 and 875 cm1 for 2 M LiFSI in DME, which is due to the mixed contributions from different C-O-C vibration modes.
In contrast, in BE the C- O-C vibration mode is more homogenized due to the high concentration of Li-ions.

When TFTFE is introduced to BE in different volume ratios, the peak of FSI stays at 735 cm1 regardless of the different ratios, indicating the consistent chemical environment of FSI ions irrespective of the volumes of TFTFE added.
Therefore, adding TFTFE into BE does not interrupt its coordination structures.

Likewise, the characteristic peaks of TFTFE at 648 cm1 and 850 cm1 remain non-shifted in HE-2 and HE-5 compared to its pure liquid, suggesting that TFTFE, indeed, serves as a diluent, not playing any solvation role with ions in the electrolytes.
AIMD was conducted to further understand the coordination structures for the electrolytes of BE and HE-2.
Solvent molecules, Li+, and FSI ions were randomly placed in the unit cell with their concentrations consistent with experiments.
Then, the unit cell was relaxed for 13 ps, in which the time between 10 ps and 15 ps is deemed sufficient to use for analysis (Figure S1).
Besides, we applied a higher energy cutoff of 600 eV for a good description of electron wavefunction [58,59].
Figure 1b illustrates the two distinctive first-coordination shells of Li+ sorted out of the entire simulation cell.

Li+ in both electrolytes is bound with three to four oxygens from DME and FSI, where the first coordination shells are analogous to the previously reported solvation structures with inert co-solvents [58,60].
To be specific, a high concentration of LiFSI renders Li+ more likely to bind with FSI rather than DME, and the oxygen atoms of TFTFE in HE-2 does not participate in the Li+ solvation.
The ions and DME already form the stable solvation structures before TFTFE is added, where less dielectric TFTFE barely perturbs the Li-O (FSI) coordination.

Furthermore, the radial distribution function (RDF) and the quantitative analysis of Li-O bonds also suggest that TFTFE functions as a diluent without involving in the coordination chemistry (Figure S2 and Table S2).
The AIMD results thereby corroborate the above Raman spectroscopy interpretation of unchanged solvation upon TFTFE addition.
The new electrolyte is designed to improve the reversibility of LMA.
We measured CE for each plating/stripping cycle by calculating the ratio of the stripped lithium over a fixed amount of plated lithium, i.e., 1.0 mAh cm2, where the current density is 0.5 mA cm2 .
Cu foil was used as a working electrode and 10 cycles of electrochemical sweeping treatment from 0.01 V to 1.0 V (vs.
Li+/Li, hereafter) at 0.05 mA cm2 was applied before lithium is initially plated (Figure S3).
For HE-2, the first plating and stripping overpotentials were respectively 35 mV and 27 mV (Figure 2a), where the CE of the initial cycle reached 96.3%.
It gradually rose to 99.6% by the 30th cycle with a reduced overpotential of 25 mV and 25 mV upon plating and stripping, respectively.
In contrast, BE exhibited an erratic behavior of plating/stripping, as shown in Figure 2b.

Initial plating/stripping overpotentials of BE were 54 mV and 45 mV, respectively, and the first CE was 93.7%, which gently increased to 97.7% by the 10th cycle, but it started to fluctuate during the following cycling.
Especially at the 26th cycle, a severe overcharge was observed with the attained capacity of 1.4 mAh cm2, 40% more than the plated amount in the same cycle.
We postulate that the extra capacity of 0.4 mAh cm2 came from the stranded Li mass over the previous cycles, which somewhat got re-wired back to the current collector in this cycle.
Figure S4 shows the GCD profiles of the six cycles, where the CE exceeds 100%.
Short circuit is typically associated with abrupt potential drops, which was not observed in these plating/stripping profiles; therefore, the high CE here is unlikely due to short circuit.
Furthermore, we tested CE of LMA in HE-2 at 2.0 mA cm2, a quadrupled current density, where dendrites may more likely form (Figure 2c).

LMA exhibited an increased extent of polarization with an initial overpotential of 190 mV that stabilized to 130 mV after 30 cycles, which is a marginally lower overpotential than the heavily fluorinated electrolytes (FEC/FEMC/HFE) and the engineered Li2S8/LiNO3 electrolyte, but slightly higher than that of using 10 M LiFSI in EC/DMC and the ternary-salt of LiFSI-LiTFSI-LiNO3 [41,61–63].
The cell showed stable potential profiles with the CE increased to 98.7% at the 30th cycle.
We tested CE over 350 cycles, and the arithmetic mean CE values are 99.4% and 99.3%, at 0.5 mA cm2 and 2.0 mA cm2, respectively, in HE-2 (Figure 2d).
The cycling stability of LMA in BE and HE-2 was also investigated in Li||Li symmetric cells at various current densities.
As observed, BE displays a greater overpotential upon plating and stripping, i.e., 31 mV, than that of HE-2, 15 mV, at 0.5 mA cm2.
The stability advantage of HE-2 is more evident at higher current densities of 1.0 mA cm2 and 2.0 mA cm2.
The results suggest the utility of TFTFE in protecting the surface of lithium metal (Figure 2e and f).
In order to understand how TFTFE as an electrolyte diluent enhances Li cycling, we investigated the surface morphology of the cycled LMA and the SEI compositions.

After 20 cycles of plating/stripping at 0.5 mA cm2 with a capacity of 1.0 mAh cm2 in Li||Li symmetric cells, LMA in HE-2 displays smooth surface with tightly bound Li grains, whereas BE shows relatively smaller Li islands with conspicuous cracks, where neither of the two electrolytes grows dendrites on LMA’s surface, as shown in Figure 3a and b.

The ratios of Li-OFSI-, Li-ODME, and Li-OTFTFE suggested by RDF analysis (Table S2) show that Li+ prefers to bind FSI over DME in both BE and in HE-2, which suggests that FSI may be preferably reduced on the LMA surface than DME.

We studied the SEI compositions by depth-profiling X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) on the cycled LMA with Ar+ sputtering that removes the top layer up to 10 nm thick beneath the surface (Figure 3c).
The N 1s spectra reveal the degree of FSI reduction on the surface of LMA in electrolytes.
The peaks at 396.8 eV and 399.1 eV can be attributed to Li-N and N-SOx, respectively, and these signals could still be found at 10 nm deep in LMA for HE-2.
However, those peaks were not detectable for BE when the top SEI layer was removed by 5 nm thick, which indicates the preferential FSI reduction on LMA in HE-2.

Besides, the F 1 s spectra demonstrate a stronger LiF peak at 685.5 eV when HE-2 is used.

Clearly, TFTFE resulted in those disparities in two folds: (1) fluorinated ethers generally exhibit lower LUMO levels compared to methyl or partially fluorinated ethers [64]; therefore, preferred defluorination of TFTFE is partially responsible for a stronger LiF peak on the LMA albeit it does not participate in the Li+ solvation; (2) Rapid TFTFE decomposition coupled with the formation of anion radicals at the Li surface triggers electron transfer to reduce FSI anions as the SEI film grows, which was recently reported by Balbuena and coworkers [65].

We cycled S@PAN||LMA half cells at the E/S ratio of 5 with excessive LMA and a sulfur loading of 2 mg cm2, where the current rate is 0.1 C (1 C = 1671 mA g1) during first seven cycles before the current rate was switched to 0.2 C for the rest of cycling.
The sulfur content of the composite was determined as 45 wt.% by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) (Table S3).
Figure 4a illustrates the galvanostatic charge– discharge (GCD) potential profiles of S@PAN in HE-2.
The sulfur mass in the S@PAN composite delivered an initial discharge capacity of 1498 mAh gs 1.

The irreversible capacity in the first discharge may relate to the formation of cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) [66] and the initial cleavage of S-S bonds, where such a reaction also induces a potential downshift [42,67].

After conditioning at 0.1 C for 7 cycles, the HE-2 cell exhibited the discharge capacity of 603 mAh gs 1 and 598 mAh gs 1 at the 10th and 50th cycle, respectively, which demonstrates the stable cycling of this S@PAN composite cathode at the E/S ratio of 5.

In sharp contrast, BE exhibited an initial discharge capacity of 952 mAh gs 1 with a lower Li-insertion potential (Figure 4b) compared to HE-2, probably due to the poor electrode wetting (Figure S5).

The discharge capacity with BE was consistently lower than HE-2 by 200 mAh g1 s , over cycling, where it delivered 407 mAh gs 1 at the 10th cycle and 386 mAh gs 1 at the 50th cycle, as shown in Figure 4c.
Interestingly, we observed that more dilution by TFTFE in HE-5 does not benefit the cycling of the sulfur cathode, as shown in Figure S6.
We postulate that this is due to the over-diluted contacting between the electrolyte-born Li+ ions and sulfur in the presence of more diluent molecules.

Encouraged by the cathode compatibility of HE-2 at the E/S ratio of 5, we assembled a full-cell Li-S battery comprising limited LMA with a N/P ratio of 2, where Li was electrochemically preplated onto a Cu current collector (Figure 4d and e).
The sulfur loading in the cathode was 3 mg cm2; the E/S ratios we tested were 3 and 2; cells were cycled at 0.05 C.
At the E/S ratio of 3, the first discharge capacity reached 1365 mAh gs 1, followed by 696 mAh gs 1 at the 10th cycle and 509 mAh gs 1 at the 50th cycle.
At the E/S ratio of 2, the cell delivered an initial discharge capacity of 1226 mAh gs 1, followed by a charge capacity of 621 mAh gs 1 with a CE of 50.7%.
In the subsequent cycles, the discharge capacity decreased to 597 mAh gs 1 and 439 mAh gs 1 at the 10th and the 50th cycle, respectively.

in Figure 4e, the discharge capacity of both E/S ratio of 3 and 2 cells faded as cycling proceeded further, which is very typical for Li-S full cells with high sulfur active mass loading under lean-electrolyte conditions.

The S@PAN||Li full cells can cycle for 100 cycles under the lean-electrolyte conditions; however, the energy density of this full cell was only 250 Wh kg1 based on the mass of both electrodes and the electrolyte, which does not deliver the promise of high energy density of Li-S batteries.

The energy density of the S@PAN||Li full cell is limited by the low average discharge voltage due to the solid–solid (S8 to Li2S) monophasic conversion reaction and the low percentage of sulfur active mass in S@PAN cathode (36 wt.%).
To investigate the applicability of HE-2 to sulfur/carbon composites, we tested the CMK-3/S cathode at the E/S ratio of 5.
An immense initial discharge capacity of 1519 mAh gs 1 and a good CE of 86% were demonstrated.
Although the capacity retained 907 mAh gs 1 at the 10th cycle, the capacity fading rate (4% per cycle) was high (Figure S7).
Plus, building a thick electrode (>5.0 mgs cm2) of this composite electrode was problematic via the conventional doctor-blade method.
Thus, we selected a hybrid cathode comprising 45 wt.% VS2 mixed with ZnS-coated Li2S@graphene, a compact composite cathode for further studies.
VS2 lowers the potential of the charge process and helps immobilize polysulfides in the electrode [68,69].

Here, we hope to cultivate the solid–liquid–solid reaction as it raises the discharge potential [31], and polysulfides can be formed because BE is not saturated with LiFSI until 12 M [19], where free DME molecules can solvate polysulfide ions, which is confirmed by the displayed yellow color of BE upon the addition of S and Li2S (stoichiometric 5:1 molar ratio, Figure S8).

ing Li+ [70], and the discharge capacity of pure VS2 was evaluated separately (Figure S9).

The entire cathode active mass loading was 7.8 mgAM cm2, and we adopted an E/S ratio of 2 by considering the ‘S’ mass in Li2S only, where the E/S ratio of 2 here is equivalent to the E/AM ratio of 0.96 mL mg1.
As shown in Figure 5a, the hybrid cathode was charged (delithiated) first to transform Li2S to elemental sulfur, which exhibited a charge capacity of 421 mAh gAM 1 from Li2S.
Upon the first discharge, nearly 20% of capacity (100 mAh gAM 1 ) was delivered at the potential of 2.3 V and above, which is mostly due to the lithiation in VS2.
The short discharge plateaus at 2.2 V and 2.0 V represent the limited formation of high-order polysulfides and their continuous reduction.
Note that the monotonous slope under 2.0 V throughout discharge is the hallmark of a solid–solid monophasic conversion [71].
Overall, the hybrid full cell exhibited an initial discharge capacity of 528 mAh gAM 1 , which corresponds to an areal capacity of 4.12 mAh cm2.

The hybrid full cell can be cycled without serious capacity fading, which maintained 82% of its initial discharge capacity for 14 cycles under the extremely lean-electrolyte conditions (Figure 5b); however, the hybrid full cell displayed noisy and extended charging profile after the 14th charge (Figure S10).

This is presumably due to the concentrated polysulfides in the parsimonious electrolyte drive a shuttle and electrolyte depletion [35,72,73], confirmed by a dried yellow-colored separator collected right after the cell failed (Figure S11), which suggests the VS2 absorption approach is still limited.
The advantage of using TFTFE as a co-solvent also lies on its unique physical properties (Table S5), particularly the flammability resistance, owing to its high flash point.
Flammability tests were conducted by placing a fire source to the electrolytesoaked glass fiber separators.
A separator soaked in HE-2 remained without fire after burning it for five consecutive seconds, and when the lighter was taken away, it showed carbonized trace on the surface (Figure S12a).
This indicates that the TFTFE addition enhances battery safety.
In contrast, the BEsoaked separator was ignited right after the lighter approached and maintained its red-yellow flame until the electrolyte was burned out (Figure S12b).
Owing to the highly combustible characteristics of DME, high salt concentration alone could not eliminate the flammability of the BE electrolyte (Video S1 and Video S2).
In a similar fashion, TFTFE also acted as a diluent, where the viscosity was drastically lowered from 107.72 mPas for BE to 11.34 mPas for HE-2.
Likewise, ionic conductivity decreases from 11.53 mS cm1 for BE to 4.59 mS cm1 for HE-2 because TFTFE does not solvate Li-ions [74] (Table S6).
The conductivity results suggest that both the diffusivity of diffusion and the mobility under the electric field of polysulfides in HE-2 and HE-5 should be smaller than in BE.
This is due to the diluent characteristics of TFTFE—a weak solvent with low permittivity, and TFTFE does not perturb the original Li+ solvation structure.
Thus, the presence of TFTFE sterically narrows the effective pathways of ions, thus lowering their movability in the electrolyte, including both Li+ and polysulfides.
Thus, the diluent may help curtail the polysulfide shuttle effect.
Conclusion In summary, we developed an electrolyte formula for the Li-S battery under lean-electrolyte conditions.
The addition of TFTFE as a co-solvent to LiFSI/DME promotes the formation of LiFabundant SEI, where the LMA exhibits a high CE of 99.4%.

The TFTFE addition also alters the physical properties of the electrolyte, where the electrolyte wets the carbon/sulfur composite cathode better, which promotes the electrolyte uptake under the lean-electrolyte conditions.
When the new electrolyte, i.e., HE-2, is paired with S@PAN cathode at a low E/S ratio of 2 and a N/P ratio of 2, the full cell can be cycled for 100 cycles.
This is a pioneering example of a full cell design, where an electrolyte facilitates excellent performance and reversibility of both electrodes under lean-electrolyte conditions.

To increase the energy density, we tested this electrolyte with a hybrid cathode, where 45 wt.% VS2 is mixed with the composite of ZnS- Li2S@graphene, which yielded an energy density of 483 Wh kg1 based on the mass of both electrodes and electrolyte.
The results here represent a new milestone achieved for the safe and highenergy density Li-S battery with a lean-electrolyte.
